content.body: Imagine placing queens on a chessboard so none can attack each other. This classic puzzle teaches a powerful problem-solving technique. Today you'll learn how to systematically explore possibilities and backtrack when needed.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Explain when and why backtracking is needed
• Implement the try → explore → undo pattern
• Solve the N-Queens problem using backtracking
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a 4×4 board. Try placing queens one row at a time. Place your first queen in row 0, column 0. Where can you safely place the next queen in row 1?
content.title: Try placing queens
content.visualMetaphor: Explore a path; if it dead-ends, go back and try another branch.

content.body: Great! You placed a queen safely in row 1. Now try row 2. Can you find a safe spot? If not, what should you do?
content.title: Continue exploring

content.body: You've reached a point where no safe spot exists in the current row. This is a dead end. What's your next move?
content.title: Hit a dead end

content.body: You tried placing queens systematically, but when you hit a dead end, you naturally wanted to go back and try different placements. That's the essence of backtracking!
content.title: What you experienced

content.body: For a 4×4 board, you can mentally track placements. But for 8×8 or larger boards, we need an algorithmic approach. We need to systematically try options and know when to backtrack.
content.title: Why we need a system

content.body: Backtracking follows a simple pattern: try a choice, explore deeper with recursion, then undo if it doesn't lead to a solution. We explore all options by undoing failed attempts and trying different branches.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Like exploring a maze: go down one path; if it's a dead end, go back to the last junction and try another path.

content.body: We'll place queens row by row. For each row, we try every column. If a placement is safe, we place the queen and recurse to the next row. If we reach the end, we found a solution. If we hit a dead end, we backtrack by removing the last queen and trying the next column.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Start from the first row
2. For each column in the current row:
   • Check if placing a queen here is safe
   • If safe: place queen, move to next row
   • If reaches last row: record solution
   • If unsafe or dead end: backtrack (remove queen)
3. Continue until all possibilities explored
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the board and results array
steps.instruction: Initialize an empty chessboard as a 2D array filled with '.' (empty spots) and an empty array to store solutions.
steps.hint: Use Array(n).fill().map(() => Array(n).fill('.')) to create the board.
steps.expectedOutcome: Board array and results array created
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up the board structure and solution container.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Remember to create both the board and results array.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's start with the basics. We need a board representation and a place to store solutions.

steps.title: Create the safety check function
steps.instruction: Write a helper function that checks if placing a queen at (row, col) is safe (no other queens in same column or diagonals).
steps.hint: Check only rows above current row since we place queens row by row.
steps.expectedOutcome: Function that checks column and diagonal conflicts
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! This safety check is crucial for valid placements.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Make sure to check all three directions: column and both diagonals.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to ensure no other queens attack this position. Check upward directions only.

steps.title: Create the backtracking function
steps.instruction: Define the recursive backtrack function that takes the current row as parameter.
steps.hint: This function will be called recursively for each row.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the recursive structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. We need a function that takes the current row.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need a function to handle the recursive exploration.

steps.title: Add base case and column iteration
steps.instruction: In the backtrack function, add the base case (all queens placed) and loop through columns in current row.
steps.hint: Base case: if row === n, we found a solution. Otherwise, try each column.
steps.expectedOutcome: Base case and column loop implemented
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up the termination condition and exploration loop.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress. Don't forget both the base case and the loop through columns.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to know when we've placed all queens and need to try each position in the current row.

steps.title: Implement try → explore → undo
steps.instruction: Inside the column loop, implement the core pattern: if safe, place queen, recurse, then remove queen (undo).
steps.hint: This is where backtracking happens: try a placement, explore deeper, then undo if it doesn't work out.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've implemented the core backtracking pattern.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Remember all three parts: try (place), explore (recurse), undo (remove).
steps.feedbackWrong: This is the heart of backtracking. We need to place a queen, explore further placements, then clean up.

steps.title: Start the backtracking and return results
steps.instruction: Call the backtrack function starting from row 0 and return the results array.
steps.hint: Initiate the recursive process and return all found solutions.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've completed the N-Queens solver using backtracking.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost done. Don't forget to start the recursion and return the solutions.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to kick off the backtracking process and return the found solutions.

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented the N-Queens solution using backtracking. Remember: backtracking is try → explore → undo. When you hit a dead end, undo the last choice and try another path. This pattern works for many constraint satisfaction problems like Sudoku, maze solving, and permutation generation.
